docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Yixiang Ren Datasheet as part of Simple Educational Robotic Arm for Team 107

Submission: Oct 30, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the Arm Motion Control subsystem of Team 107's robotic arm, designed by Yixiang Ren for EGR 304 Embedded Systems Design at Arizona State University. It collects the design work for this one board: the block diagram, how each part was chosen, the bill of materials, the schematic and the power budget. A reader can use it to understand, build, test or modify the board without other documents.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Team 107 is building a Simple Educational Robotic Arm: a low-cost desktop arm that performs repeatable pick-and-place tasks and is meant for students, educators and hobbyists who are learning robotics and embedded systems. The system is split into three boards, each with its own PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, linked in a daisy chain by an 8-pin ribbon cable:

Board Owner Role Arm Motion Control (this datasheet) Yixiang Ren Drives the arm joint motor and reports when the arm is in position Gripper & Object Handling Canyon Miller Opens and closes the gripper and senses the held object User Controls & Safety Dunyue Yang Start, stop and speed inputs, status LEDs and buzzer

The full project, including user needs, product requirements, the team block diagram and the software proposal, is in the Team 107 report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
The Arm Motion Control board turns commands from the team into arm movement:

  • Power: it takes a 9 V wall adapter, protects the input with a fuse and a reverse-polarity diode, and makes a 6 V motor rail (LM317T) and a 5 V logic rail (L7805).
  • Motor drive: an onsemi FAN8100N H-bridge drives a 6 V Pololu micro gearmotor in both directions, with speed set by PWM from the PIC.
  • Team link: on the ribbon cable it reads SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, OBJ_HELD and the analog SPEED_SET, and it sends GRIP_CMD and ARM_IN_POS. An unplugged cable reads as "stop".
  • Debug and expansion: a status LED, a push button, test points on both rails and a spare-I/O header (J4) make the board easy to test and to extend.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram shows the blocks of the Arm Motion Control board, how power and signals move between them, and how the board connects to the rest of the team.

  • Microcontroller: the board runs on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The Nano is powered from its own USB port and uses 3.3 V logic with a 0–3.3 V analog range.
  • Power: a 9 V DC wall adapter plugs into a barrel jack.
    • The input goes through a 1 A slow-blow fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode.
    • An LM317T, set by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω, makes the 6.0 V motor rail.
    • An L7805 makes the 5 V logic rail.
    • Motor current never passes through the microcontroller board.
    • In the diagram, the power path is drawn only from the source to the regulators. Blocks that receive power have no supply lines pointing to them; instead the rail each block runs from is written in bold inside it (for example PVCC +6 V / VCC +5 V on the H-bridge, 3.3 V on the LED, button and J4).
  • Actuator: an onsemi FAN8100N H-bridge drives a 6 V Pololu #2370 DC gearmotor. The motor has two wires, M+ and M−. RB0 and RB1 provide the two PWM inputs through PPS.
  • Debug:
    • A status LED on RE0.
    • A push button on RE1, using the weak pull-up.
    • Expansion header J4, which brings out 3.3 V, GND and the spare pins RA0, RA2, RB2 and RB3.
  • Team connection: the board connects to the Gripper & Object Handling board through the 8-pin ribbon cable.
    • It receives SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, OBJ_HELD and the analog SPEED_SET.
    • It sends GRIP_CMD and ARM_IN_POS.
    • Pin 7 (GRIP_FORCE) is not used on this board and is left open. Pin 8 is GND.
  • Ground: all grounds are tied together. This includes USB, the 9 V supply, the H-bridge and ribbon pin 8.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page records how each major part of the Arm Motion Control board was chosen. For every function, at least three options were compared, the decision is stated, and the reason is tied to the team's product requirements (PR numbers from the team report). Several choices changed after the first submission; each section says what changed and why.

The same criteria were used for every part:

Criterion Why it matters Related requirements Current and voltage ratings above the worst case in this circuit, with margin Parts must stay inside their limits, including at motor stall PR-14, Regulation 6.7 Fits the class rules: through-hole (nothing smaller than 0805), not obsolete when ordered, full datasheet, no breakout module without approval The board must be hand-soldered, prototyped on a breadboard and reviewed PR-10, PR-14 Uses parts already in hand or stocked in Peralta 109 where possible Keeps the subsystem inside the team budget PR-17 Simple interface to the PIC18F57Q43 (few pins, no extra drivers) Easier firmware and easier for students to follow PR-07, PR-15, PR-16 Leaves room to add parts later (sockets, spare pins, header) The arm is meant to be modified and expanded PR-10, PR-11 Fails safe (protection features, known state when unplugged) Motion must stop predictably PR-12, Regulation 6.3 / 6.7

docs.title: H-Bridge Motor Driver
docs.text:
1. Pololu DRV8874 single brushed DC motor driver carrier

    • $11.94/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons PH/EN mode controls speed and direction with one PWM pin plus one GPIO, which matches our pin map. Most expensive of the three drivers. Integrated current sensing and regulation (IPROPI, VREF) limits motor current without an external shunt resistor. Needs PMODE and nSLEEP wired, which adds two connections compared with a two-input driver. Undervoltage, overcurrent and thermal protection, plus an nFAULT output the firmware can read. Includes 0.1" breakaway headers, so it can be hand soldered and tested on a breadboard.

  2. Adafruit DRV8871 DC motor driver breakout

    • $7.50/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lower price Changing the current limit means swapping a resistor, not changing a reference voltage. Current limit set by a resistor, so the motor is protected without firmware. No current-sense output for the firmware to read Simple two-input interface and well documented by Adafruit.

  3. TB6612FNG Dual Motor Driver Carrier

    • $4.95/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest price No current sensing or regulation. Two channels, so the second channel could be paralleled for 2 A continuous or kept as a spare. Three control inputs per channel plus a shared STBY pin, it uses more GPIO than our pin map 3 A peak current and PWM frequencies up to 100 kHz.

  4. onsemi (Fairchild) FAN8100N low-voltage dual-channel DC motor driver, 12-DIPH-300 with heat-sink fin (selected)

    • Already in hand (two parts), so $0 to the order
    • Datasheet
    Pros Cons Through-hole DIP with a heat-sink fin: fits the breadboard and the PCB directly, no breakout module needed. Obsolete, so it cannot be reordered; the two parts in hand cover the breadboard and the PCB. 1.5 A peak output per channel, more than twice the 0.67 A motor stall current. No current-sense output for the firmware. Two logic inputs per channel (forward / reverse), driven directly by two PWM pins (RB0, RB1). Bipolar output stage drops about 0.15 V at 0.2 A and up to 0.55 V at 0.4 A, so the motor sees slightly less than 6 V. Built-in thermal shutdown with hysteresis and built-in clamp ("spark killing") diodes, so no external flyback diodes. Supply limit is 9 V (10.5 V absolute), so it suits only low-voltage motors. Separate logic (VCC) and power (PVCC) supplies: 5 V logic, 6 V motor rail.

Choice: Option 4, onsemi FAN8100N.

Rationale: The first submission chose the DRV8874 carrier for a 12 V, 5 A-stall motor. When the design moved to the 6 V micro gearmotor (0.67 A stall), that much driver was no longer needed, and all three earlier options are breakout modules, which the class asks us not to order without approval. The FAN8100N is a bare through-hole IC that is already in hand (PR-17), it is rated above the motor stall current (PR-14), and its thermal shutdown and internal clamp diodes protect the board if the motor stalls (Regulation 6.7). Its forward / reverse inputs map to two PWM outputs, so speed and direction are set with two pins and no extra logic (PR-07, PR-15). It sits in a socket, so it can be replaced without soldering (PR-10). Only channel A is used; channel B inputs are tied to ground.

docs.title: DC Motor
docs.text:
1. 34:1 Metal Gearmotor 25Dx67L mm HP 12V with 48 CPR Encoder

    • $56.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 11 kg·cm stall torque at 300 rpm no-load speed gives the most torque margin Most expensive option Built-in two-channel Hall-effect quadrature encoder Stall current is 5.0 A, above the driver's continuous rating Datasheet and dimension drawing are available for the mechanical design Adds mass to the arm; the weight is not listed on the page and must be checked 4 mm D-shaft output. The encoder needs a 3.5 V to 20 V supply and its outputs swing from 0 V to Vcc

  2. Pololu 250:1 Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V

    • $23.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Very compact with metal gears, saves arm weight. Stall torque is only 1.6 kg·cm, about one seventh of Option 1 Low stall current fits any of the three drivers. Manufacturer warns that stalling can damage the motor or gearbox The extended motor shaft allows a magnetic encoder to be added later. No encoder included Datasheet available

  3. Adafruit DC gearbox "TT" motor, 200 rpm, 3 to 6 VDC

    • $2.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest price Stall torque is only 0.8 kg·cm at 6 V, too low for a loaded arm joint. Light with a 1:48 gearbox and 200 mm leads ending in 0.1" connectors. Rated 3 V to 6 V, needs a separate lower-voltage rail. Low current (1.5 A stall at 6 V). No encoder included; only a basic specification sheet, no full datasheet.

Choice: Option 2, Pololu 250:1 Micro Metal Gearmotor MP 6V.

Rationale: Its 0.67 A stall current is within the FAN8100N (1.5 A) and the LM317T 6 V regulator (1.5 A) with margin, so the whole motor path stays inside its ratings (PR-14, see the Power Budget). Option 1 needs 5 A at stall, which would need a much larger driver and supply. Its 1.6 kg·cm stall torque is about twice that of the TT motor, which gives margin while the arm load is still being defined, and its metal gears and small size keep the arm light and stable (PR-04, PR-13). At $23.95 it is far cheaper than Option 1 (PR-17). The extended back shaft leaves room to add an encoder later (PR-11).

docs.title: Position Sensor
docs.text:
1. Bourns 6639S-1-103, 10 kΩ single-turn conductive plastic precision potentiometer

    • $24.77/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Single analog output goes straight to RA0, using one pin and no driver code. Highest price of the three position sensors The reading is still valid after power loss, so no homing routine is needed. Mechanical contact wear over time. Not affected by the magnetic field of the motor. The wiper can be noisy, so the firmware should average several ADC samples. Used as a divider between 3.3 V and GND, the ±15% resistance tolerance does not matter because the reading is ratiometric.

  2. Bourns 3590S-2-103L, 10 kΩ 10-turn wirewound precision potentiometer

    • $17.78/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lower price than Option 1 a joint that moves less than one revolution would use only a small part of the range, which wastes ADC resolution unless it is geared up. ±0.25% independent linearity, the best of the three. Wirewound elements change resistance in small steps rather than continuously. 2 W power rating and a −40 °C to +125 °C operating range. Larger body and a gear or pulley train would be needed, adding mechanical complexity

  3. Adafruit AS5600 magnetic angle sensor (STEMMA QT)

    • $5.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Lowest cost Needs a diametrically magnetized magnet centered on the shaft axis Contactless, so there is no wear The motor's magnets and currents can disturb the magnetic reading 12-bit absolute angle (4096 steps per revolution) Whether the analog OUT pin is available on this board must be confirmed Can be read over I2C or analog voltage. More design work needed

Choice: No position sensor in the current design (Rev B onward).

Rationale: After the first submission the team simplified the arm board, and the position sensor was removed so that the first prototype has fewer parts and less firmware. The arm moves the joint at a set PWM duty for a set time and then raises ARM_IN_POS on the ribbon cable. To keep the option open (PR-11), analog-capable pin RA0 (ANA0) and 3.3 V are brought out on expansion header J4, so Option 1 or Option 3 can be added later without changing the PCB.

docs.title: Motor Power Source
docs.text:
1. Mean Well GST60A12-P1J, 12 V 5 A desktop AC adapter

    • $19.40/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Regulated 12 V at 5 A with 120 mVp-p ripple, no extra voltage regulator is needed on the motor rail. The AC inlet is IEC C14, so a power cord must be purchased separately Overload and over voltage protection. At the motor's 5 A stall current the supply would be at 100% of its rating, no margin 2.1 × 5.5 mm barrel plug and 4,059 units in stock Tethered to a wall outlet, not portable Full datasheet is available

  2. Adafruit 12 V 5 A switching power supply

    • $24.95/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 12 V at up to 5 A with a 2.1 mm barrel plug on about a 40 inch cable. The page listed it as out of stock when checked UL approved and RoHS compliant More expensive than Option 1 for the same rating Datasheet No clear datasheet is provided on the product page

  3. Tenergy 12 V 2000 mAh NiMH battery pack (10S1P)

    • $36.49/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Portable, the arm can run without a wall outlet Maximum continuous discharge is 2 A, below the motor's stall current 12 V nominal at 2000 mAh (24 Wh) Voltage sags as the cells discharge and rises when fully charged Rechargeable Highest price No separate datasheet and a suitable charger must also be bought

  4. MEAN WELL GST25A09-P1J, 9 V 2.55 A desktop AC adapter (selected)

    • $13.70/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons 9 V is just enough for the LM317T to make 6 V after the reverse-polarity diode (8.55 V available, about 8 V needed). Needs a separate IEC C13 power cord (also on the BOM). 2.55 A rating, well above the 947 mA worst-case input current. Low stock at Mouser (37 when checked), so it should be ordered early. Lower voltage than a 12 V supply, so VR1 dissipates about 2.4 W instead of about 5 W. Tethered to a wall outlet, not portable. Short-circuit, overload and over-voltage protection; full datasheet; 2.1 × 5.5 mm plug.

Choice: Option 4, MEAN WELL GST25A09-P1J.

Rationale: The first submission chose a 12 V 5 A adapter for the 12 V motor. With the 6 V motor, the Power Budget shows a worst-case input current of about 947 mA, so 5 A is not needed, and a lower input voltage keeps the 6 V linear regulator cool: (8.55 V − 6 V) × 0.93 A ≈ 2.4 W at 9 V, compared with about 5 W from 12 V. The 9 V supply still leaves enough headroom for the LM317T dropout. It is a regulated, protected, low-voltage desktop supply (Regulation 6.1), it costs less than the 12 V options (PR-17), and the battery pack was rejected because it cannot deliver stall current and needs a charger.

docs.title: Voltage Regulation
docs.text:
The board needs a 6 V motor rail and a 5 V logic rail from the 9 V input. The 3.3 V logic rail is made by the MIC5353 regulator on the Curiosity Nano, which runs from USB.

  1. STMicroelectronics L7806CV, fixed 6 V regulator, TO-220

    Pros Cons Fixed 6 V output, no external resistors. L7806CV, L7806ABV and MC7806 are listed as obsolete or not orderable at Mouser, and ordering obsolete parts is a listed common mistake.

  2. STMicroelectronics LM317T, adjustable regulator, TO-220 (selected for the 6 V rail, VR1)

    • $0.76/each, link to product
    Pros Cons In stock and cheap; 1.5 A output, current limit, thermal shutdown. Needs two resistors: R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω give Vout = 1.25 V × (1 + 910 / 240) = 6.0 V. Output can be trimmed if the motor needs a different voltage. Needs about 2 V of headroom and a heat sink at full load (2.4 W).

  3. STMicroelectronics L7805CV, fixed 5 V regulator, TO-220 (selected for the 5 V rail, VR2)

    • $0.60/each, link to product
    Pros Cons Fixed 5 V, 1.5 A, current limit and thermal shutdown; only 0.33 µF in and 0.1 µF out. Linear regulator wastes power as heat, which is negligible at about 14 mA (0.08 W).

Choice: LM317T for the 6 V motor rail and L7805CV for the 5 V logic rail.

Rationale: A fixed 6 V regulator would be simplest, but none was orderable, so the LM317T is set to 6.0 V with two 1 % resistors. Both regulators are TO-220 through-hole parts with built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown (PR-14, Regulation 6.7), and both are cheap and in stock (PR-17). The power budget sets the heat sink for VR1 and confirms that VR2 needs none. Keeping the motor rail and logic rail on separate regulators stops motor current spikes from disturbing the FAN8100N logic supply.

docs.title: Microcontroller and MCC Configuration
docs.text:
The team uses the Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano (DM164150) on every board. It is powered and programmed over USB, runs at 3.3 V, and plugs into female headers so it can be removed (PR-10). The table below is the MCC configuration for this board: every peripheral and pin the Arm Motion Control firmware uses.

Function MCC module Pin Direction Settings System clock Clock Control — — HFINTOSC, 64 MHz Motor forward PWM (MOT_FWD → FAN8100N FORWARDA) PWM1 (16-bit PWM), routed with PPS RB0 Output Duty cycle sets speed; 0 % when stopped; R8 100 kΩ pull-down holds the input low during reset Motor reverse PWM (MOT_REV → FAN8100N REVERSEA) PWM1 second output, routed with PPS RB1 Output Only one of RB0 / RB1 is active at a time; R9 100 kΩ pull-down SPEED_SET (ribbon pin 6) ADCC RA1 (ANA1) Analog input 12-bit, VDD reference; 1 kΩ / 0.1 µF RC filter on the board SAFE_OK (ribbon pin 1) Pin Manager (GPIO) RD0 Digital input External 10 kΩ pull-down, weak pull-up off RUN_REQ (ribbon pin 2) Pin Manager (GPIO) RD1 Digital input External 10 kΩ pull-down, weak pull-up off GRIP_CMD (ribbon pin 3) Pin Manager (GPIO) RD2 Digital output 330 Ω series resistor, starts low OBJ_HELD (ribbon pin 4) Pin Manager (GPIO) RD3 Digital input External 10 kΩ pull-down, weak pull-up off ARM_IN_POS (ribbon pin 5) Pin Manager (GPIO) RD4 Digital output 330 Ω series resistor, starts low Debug LED DS2 Pin Manager (GPIO) RE0 Digital output 330 Ω to the LED, about 3.6 mA Debug button SW1 Pin Manager (GPIO) RE1 Digital input Weak pull-up on (WPUE1 = 1), pressed = 0, debounced in firmware Expansion header J4 — RA0, RA2, RB2, RB3 Not used yet Left as inputs; RA0 / RA2 are analog-capable for a future sensor Ribbon pin 7 (GRIP_FORCE) — — Not connected Not used on this board

The three ribbon inputs read 0 when the cable is unplugged, which the firmware treats as "stop", and both motor PWM outputs start at 0 % on reset, so the motor cannot move until SAFE_OK and RUN_REQ are high (PR-12).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page lists every component of the Arm Motion Control subsystem, taken from the subsystem schematic. It also lists the off-board items the system needs to run and the debugging and expansion hardware.

How the quantities were chosen:

  • One set for a breadboard prototype, one set for the subsystem PCB, and one or two spares, as the assignment asks.
  • Through-hole parts only (nothing smaller than 0805), so every part can be hand-soldered and used on a breadboard.
  • Parts that are in hand, handed out in class or kept in Peralta 109 (resistors, LEDs, fuses, IC sockets, headers) are still listed, but they are not on a purchase request.

The table is sorted by vendor, one section per purchase request. Prices and stock were checked on the vendor pages on 2026-10-30 and should be re-checked before the order is sent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the Arm Motion Control subsystem of Team 107 Simple Educational Robotic Arm. It is drawn in KiCad 9 with US/ANSI symbols, and parts are joined by wires rather than net labels wherever possible, so the signal path can be followed by eye. The sheet has five blocks:

  • Power: a 9 V DC barrel jack feeds a 1 A slow-blow fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity Schottky diode, giving VIN_PROT of about 8.55 V. VR1 is an LM317T set to 6.0 V by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω, using Vout = 1.25 V × (1 + 910 / 240) = 6.0 V. This 6 V rail is the motor rail. VR2 makes the +5 V logic rail for the H-bridge VCC and the power LED DS1. Each regulator has 0.33 µF on its input and 0.1 µF on its output. Test points TP1 and TP2 are on the 6 V and 5 V rails.
  • Microcontroller: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, powered from its own USB port with 3.3 V logic.
  • Motor drive: an onsemi FAN8100N H-bridge drives the 6 V Pololu #2370 gearmotor through M+ and M−. The motor has only these two pins. RB0 and RB1 supply PWM through PPS. The motor supply has 47 µF and 0.1 µF bulk and decoupling capacitors.
  • Debug and expansion:
    • A status LED on RE0.
    • A push button on RE1, using the weak pull-up.
    • J4, a 6-pin expansion header carrying 3.3 V, GND, RA0, RA2, RB2 and RB3.
  • Team ribbon: pins 1 to 8 carry, in order:
    • SAFE_OK (in)
    • RUN_REQ (in)
    • GRIP_CMD (out)
    • OBJ_HELD (in)
    • ARM_IN_POS (out)
    • SPEED_SET (analog in)
    • pin 7, which is not used on this board
    • GND

The three digital inputs have 10 kΩ pull-downs, so an unplugged cable reads 0, which means stop. The two outputs have 330 Ω series resistors. SPEED_SET has a 1 kΩ / 0.1 µF RC filter.

Figure 1: Arm Motion Control schematic (click the image to enlarge).

docs.title: 3.3 V Operation Check
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 on this board runs at 3.3 V. It is powered by the Curiosity Nano's own MIC5353 regulator from USB, and the VTG pin (+3V3 in the schematic) is that regulator's output. Nothing on this board drives VTG. Every connection to the PIC was checked against 3.3 V operation:

Check Requirement Result PIC18F57Q43 supply range Operating voltage 1.8 V – 5.5 V (PIC18-Q43 family product brief) 3.3 V is inside the range ✔ Curiosity Nano target voltage MIC5353 adjustable 1.8 V – 5.1 V, set to 3.3 V at the factory (user guide, sec. 3.3.1 "Target Regulator") Leave the target voltage at 3.3 V in the MPLAB X project properties ✔ Regulator current 3.3 V loads need about 99 mA with margin (Power Budget); MIC5353 supplies 500 mA ✔ PIC → FAN8100N inputs (RB0, RB1) FAN8100N input high ≥ 1.8 V, input low ≤ 0.7 V, input current ≤ 200 µA; datasheet lists "3.3 V and 5 V micro-controller interface" (datasheet) A 3.3 V output is well above 1.8 V. The FAN8100N logic supply is 5 V, but its inputs only need 1.8 V, so no level shifter is needed ✔ SPEED_SET analog input (RA1) ADC reference = VDD = 3.3 V; the User board's speed knob also runs from its Nano's 3.3 V, so the signal is 0 – 3.3 V ✔ Ribbon signals to and from the other boards All three boards use PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nanos at 3.3 V, so every logic level on the ribbon is 0 / 3.3 V ✔ All three Nanos must stay at 3.3 V. If one board's target voltage were changed to 5 V, its outputs would exceed this PIC's 3.3 V supply. Debug LED DS2 on RE0 (3.3 V − 2.1 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 3.6 mA, a small load for one I/O pin ✔ Debug button SW1 on RE1 Internal weak pull-up to 3.3 V; the button pulls to GND ✔ J4 3.3 V pin Comes from VTG, so an add-on sensor runs at the same 3.3 V logic level as the PIC ✔

The only 5 V and 6 V nets on the board are the FAN8100N supply pins (VCC, PVCC), the motor and the power LED. None of them connects to a PIC pin.

docs.title: How the Schematic Meets the User Needs and Product Requirements
docs.text:
The team grouped its user needs into eleven categories and turned them into product requirements PR-01 to PR-18 (user needs, product requirements). The table shows which parts of this schematic serve each need that applies to the Arm Motion Control board, and how.

User need category Requirements What in the schematic serves it How it works Safety PR-12, PR-14, Reg. 6.3, 6.7 R2, R3, R5 pull-downs on SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, OBJ_HELD; R8, R9 pull-downs on the H-bridge inputs; F1; D1; FAN8100N thermal shutdown If the ribbon cable is unplugged or the User board drops SAFE_OK, the inputs read 0 and the firmware stops the motor. R8 and R9 hold both H-bridge inputs low while the PIC resets, so the motor cannot twitch at power-up. F1 (1 A slow-blow) opens on a short, D1 blocks a reversed adapter, and the FAN8100N shuts down if it overheats during a stall. Accuracy & Repeatability PR-01, PR-02, PR-04 VR1 LM317T regulated 6 V rail; C6, C7 on the motor supply; PWM on RB0 / RB1 The motor always sees a regulated 6.0 V (set by 1 % resistors R11 / R12) instead of a raw adapter voltage, so the same PWM duty gives the same speed every run. Bulk and bypass capacitors keep the rail steady when the motor starts. Programming & Control PR-07, PR-16 FAN8100N forward / reverse inputs on two PWM pins; SPEED_SET on RA1 (ADC) Speed and direction are two duty-cycle values, which is easy for a student to change in code and see on the arm. SPEED_SET from the User board is read by the ADC through a 1 kΩ / 0.1 µF filter, so the speed knob gives a smooth reading. Gripper & Object Handling (team link) PR-01, PR-03 J3 ribbon: GRIP_CMD and ARM_IN_POS outputs with R4, R6 (330 Ω); OBJ_HELD input The arm tells the gripper when to close and reports when it is in position, and it waits for OBJ_HELD before moving on. The 330 Ω resistors limit current if two boards ever drive the same wire. Documentation & Troubleshooting PR-09, PR-18 TP1 (+6 V), TP2 (+5 V); power LED DS1; debug LED DS2 on RE0; button SW1 on RE1 DS1 shows at a glance that the 5 V rail is up. The test points let a user check both rails with a meter. DS2 and SW1 let the firmware show its state and step through a sequence during troubleshooting. Sensors, Vision & Expansion PR-10, PR-11 J4 header (3.3 V, GND, RA0, RA2, RB2, RB3); unused FAN8100N channel B A sensor such as a joint potentiometer or magnetic encoder can be added on J4 (RA0 and RA2 are analog-capable) without a new PCB. The second H-bridge channel is available for a second motor. Calibration, Maintenance & Repair PR-05, PR-10 U1 in a socket; Curiosity Nano on female headers; J2 screw terminal for the motor The driver, the MCU board and the motor can each be replaced without desoldering. Assembly, Wiring & Components PR-10, PR-14 All through-hole parts; keyed 2×4 shrouded header J3; parts run within ratings The board can be hand-soldered and built on a breadboard first. The keyed header prevents the ribbon from being plugged in backwards. The Power Budget shows every part stays within its limits. Power, Stability & Physical Design PR-13, PR-14, Reg. 6.1 9 V adapter, VR1 with heat sink, VR2, separate motor and logic rails Everything runs from a low-voltage desktop adapter. The motor and the logic have separate regulators, so motor noise does not reach the logic supply, and VR1's heat sink keeps it cool at stall. Cost & Accessibility PR-15, PR-17 FAN8100N and passives already in hand; common TO-220 regulators The parts to order cost $128.35 in total, and every part is a common, documented through-hole component.

Signal path, start to finish: the User board raises SAFE_OK and RUN_REQ → the PIC reads SPEED_SET on the ADC and drives PWM on RB0 (forward) or RB1 (reverse) → the FAN8100N switches the 6 V rail across the motor → when the move is done the PIC raises ARM_IN_POS and GRIP_CMD → the Gripper board answers on OBJ_HELD → the arm moves to the place position. At any point, SAFE_OK going low sets both PWM outputs to 0 % and the motor stops.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This power budget checks that every supply and regulator on the Arm Motion Control board can deliver the worst-case current its loads can draw, with a 25 % safety margin. It is filled in on the power budget template from the original assignment. The board has two independent sources, and their grounds are tied together on the board:

  • 9 V wall adapter (MEAN WELL GST25A09-P1J, 2.55 A) → J1 → F1 (1 A slow-blow) → D1 (1N5819), giving about 8.55 V. This feeds two regulators:
    • +6 V motor rail: VR1, an LM317T set by R11 = 240 Ω and R12 = 910 Ω. It feeds the FAN8100N output stage and the Pololu #2370 6 V gearmotor.
    • +5 V logic rail: VR2, an L7805CV. It feeds the FAN8100N logic (VCC) and the power LED DS1.
  • USB port of the PC (500 mA) → the Curiosity Nano's MIC5353 LDO → the +3.3 V rail for the PIC18F57Q43, the debug LED, the ribbon outputs and expansion header J4.

How the numbers were chosen:

  • The major-component table lists each active part with its absolute maximum current from its datasheet: FAN8100N 1.5 A peak per channel, motor stall 0.67 A, Curiosity Nano regulator 500 mA, and LED forward-current ratings.
  • The rail tables use the worst case each part can draw in this circuit. The motor is counted at its 0.67 A stall current. The FAN8100N is counted at its maximum supply current (65 mA PVCC, 8 mA VCC). The LEDs are counted at the current their resistors allow.
  • Two values are design allowances rather than datasheet figures, and they are marked "allow." in the sheet: 25 mA for the MCU core and 50 mA reserved on the J4 3.3 V pin.
  • On the external-source tables, the loads are each rail's required current (with margin), not the regulators' 1.5 A ratings. Adding the two ratings (3 A) would exceed the 2.55 A adapter even though the real demand is below 1 A.

Figure 1: Power budget, page 1. Major components and the +6 V motor rail.

Figure 2: Power budget, page 2. +5 V logic rail and +3.3 V rail.

Figure 3: Power budget, page 3. External power sources, battery life (not applicable) and notes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The budget shows the following:

  • Every rail and source has headroom at worst case. The tightest point is the +6 V rail, where motor stall plus margin uses about 62 % of the LM317T's 1.5 A rating.
  • The fuse is sized correctly. Worst-case input current through F1 is about 947 mA, under the 1 A rating. F1 is slow-blow, so it rides through motor start-up and short stalls, but it still opens on a sustained fault. In normal running the motor draws about 0.1–0.2 A, far below this.
  • VR1 needs a heatsink. At worst case it dissipates (8.55 − 6) V × 0.93 A ≈ 2.4 W, which is too much for a bare TO-220. The Aavid 577102B00000G heatsink is in the BOM. VR2 dissipates only about 0.08 W and needs none.
  • The FAN8100N stays well inside its limits. Its 1.5 A per-channel output rating is more than twice the motor's stall current. Its estimated saturation loss at stall, about 0.6 W, is under the 2.0 W package rating.
  • The 9 V input gives the LM317T enough dropout margin. After the reverse-polarity diode the input is 8.55 V, and the LM317T needs about 6 V + 2 V = 8 V.
  • One small risk is the LM317T minimum load. The R11 / R12 divider draws 5.2 mA. That is above the typical 3.5 mA minimum load in the datasheet but below its 10 mA worst case. With the motor off, the 6 V rail could drift slightly high. If this shows up on the bench, a smaller divider (for example R11 = 120 Ω, R12 = 453 Ω) fixes it.

How the budget shaped the design: it is the reason the 6 V rail uses an LM317T with a heat sink and not a bare regulator, the reason the input supply is 9 V (high enough for the LM317T dropout, low enough to keep VR1 under about 2.4 W; a 12 V adapter would push VR1 to about 5 W), and the reason F1 is a 1 A slow-blow fuse. It also confirmed that the Curiosity Nano can stay on USB power, because the 3.3 V loads need only about 99 mA of its 500 mA regulator.
